subject: Removing details from file when saving sampling chain

messages.author: 7dd668eb41c5bfd9
messages.subject: Removing details from file when saving sampling chain
parts:
Hi all,

I'm running a rather large model (around 2K parameters) with 5,000 posterior samples for each parameter. I've been running the model on a remote cluster, saving the sampling output from PySTAN using the sample_file argument:

model.sampling(..., sample_file='chains')

to save a CSV of the posteriors from each chain. I then load the chains into Python on my personal computer to plot coefficients, examine convergence, and do all of the necessary backend work.

The problem is that the sample_file output adds extra rows (like #Sample generated by Stan, #stan_version_major) at the top, and halfway through where the burn-in iterations cease there is a row break for #adaptation terminated, etc. Normally, I can open the posteriors in Excel and delete the extra rows, along with the adaptation samples, so that my posteriors can be read into Python or R. However, for my current files (2K columns, 10K rows) this is impossible. The file size is nearly 2 GB (above the internal limit for 32-bit Excel), and other programs without file size limits like LibreOffice put a limit on the number of columns. The result being that I cannot find a spreadsheet program capable of opening the sample_files to delete the extra rows and adaptation steps.

I've looked, but I've found no option in the PySTAN API that allows sample_files to ignore writing the details and, ideally, burn-in steps. Is this possible, or planned?

Also, the logical solution would be to get 64-bit Excel, which does not have a file size limit, and open the chains. But Microsoft does not (or will not) make a 64-bit version of Office for Mac. The newest 2016 Office for Mac is still 32-bit. So this seems like an issue that is not easily solvable at the moment.

Any advice for how to get around this issue?

Nate

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Removing details from file when saving sampling chain [pystan]
parts:
Why do you want to use Excel? (That wasn't rhetorical --- I'm
really curious why you'd ever load one of these files into Excel.)

If you set the comment character in Excel, it should delete the
extra rows for you. It's just an ordinary CSV file with "#" as
the line comment.

You should be able to set PyStan so it doesn't save warmup (don't
let Andrew hear you say "burnin" :-)). If not, please create an
issue on stan-dev/pystan.

The formats are going to get cleaned up and the options for
running Stan unified across interfaces in Stan 3. But that's
still a long way off.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Removing details from file when saving sampling chain
parts:
On Tuesday, February 23, 2016 at 12:01:20 PM UTC-5, Nathan Lemoine wrote:
Any advice for how to get around this issue?

You can also use sed or something on the remote server to separate the comment lines from the other lines.

grep "^#" chains*.csv > comments.txt
sed -i '/^#/d' chains*.csv

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Removing details from file when saving sampling chain
parts:
Be careful what you grep and sed if you're not used to these tools.

Ben saves the comments here first before overwriting chains*.csv.
This may cause them to be unreadable by other Stan tools (at least
as they stand now). Doesn't RStan use the comments in some way
to determine things like which rows are warmup?

So if you can afford the storage space, I'd try to avoid
overwriting chains.csv. I don't know how easy that is to
do with sed or awk or Python.

- Bob

messages.author: 7dd668eb41c5bfd9
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Removing details from file when saving sampling chain
parts:
Hi.

Thanks for all of the help. I was using Excel to delete the commented lines so that the files could be read into Python (or R). Trying to read files in led to errors because of the extra lines. However, after Bob’s initial comment, I searched the help docs and found that it’s possible to exclude lines with a comment symbol. I had no idea this was possible, and it completely solved my situation.

To answer Bob’s original question about why I’d use Excel, I wouldn’t and probably never will any more now that I know I don’t have to.

Thanks!

Nate
